title: Scalable Exact Non-Pauli Noise Simulation for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum design relies on simulating noisy quantum error correction (QEC) circuits with hundreds to thousands of physical qubits and large circuit depths. High-throughput stabilizer simulators, such as Stim, are the de facto tools for this regime. However, these simulators typically support only Clifford gates and stochastic Pauli noise. As a result, more realistic device noise models-such as coherent control errors and thermal relaxation-are often approximated using Pauli Twirling. This replacement offers speed but can introduce inaccuracies. To address this, we propose QuasiStim for scalable exact QEC simulation of realistic noise, with QuasiFold as a compiler frontend and DeltaFrame as a sampling backend. QuasiFold lowers sampling overhead by merging equivalent non-Pauli sites in the quantum circuit. DeltaFrame samples the resulting stabilizer trajectories by reusing precomputed predicted references instead of resimulating the full tableau for each shot. QuasiFold can reduce the number of shots by over $100\times$ on bivariate-bicycle (BB) codes. Compared to a per-shot tableau simulator, DeltaFrame is $166\times$--$1331\times$ faster on rotated surface-code memory under coherent $R_Z$ noise as $d$ grows from 5 to 35. QuasiStim also makes the PTA bias measurable: the gap is non-negligible and varies with noise strength, decoder, and circuit schedule. QuasiStim will be open-sourced upon publication at https://github.com/isaachyw/QuasiStim

title: Benchmarking a randomized quantum algorithm for estimating expectation values of molecular observables
summary: Randomized quantum algorithms for the estimation of expectation values of molecular observables offer a promising route to early fault-tolerant quantum advantage by trading circuit depth for an increased number of samples. However, this begs the question whether the resulting measurement overhead remains feasible for industrially relevant molecular systems. In this work, we benchmark the randomized sampling algorithm of Wang et al. [1] through numerical simulations on a hydrogen molecule and resource estimates for various active spaces of the cytochrome P450, an industry-relevant system in the pharmaceutical industry. Our numerical simulations reveal that the analytical error bounds significantly overestimate the actual sampling error, whereas the analytical bound on the required imaginary evolution time is comparatively tight, exceeding a direct DMRG estimate by roughly 44% for the active space where the comparison is feasible. The measurement overhead nevertheless remains prohibitively high: even for the smallest active spaces, the expectation-value estimation alone requires around 1010 samples, scaling to beyond 1015 for the largest active spaces considered. These results suggest that substantial improvements in measurement strategies or algorithmic scaling are necessary before randomized early-fault-tolerant algorithms become competitive for industrial quantum chemistry applications.

title: Magic-Free Certification of Logical Error Rates in Universal Fault-Tolerant Circuits
summary: As quantum hardware enters the fault-tolerant regime, algorithms are beginning to be executed on encoded qubits, yet scalable certification of how well they run remains an open problem. Here we introduce magic-free certification, a certification protocol for universal fault-tolerant circuits that consumes no magic, the resource that generally places them beyond efficient classical simulation and is by far the most expensive element of a fault-tolerant computation. The protocol is code- and decoder-agnostic, runs interleaved with the target circuit on the same device, and has a sample complexity that grows linearly with the number of logical qubits and non-Clifford gates while remaining decoupled from the logical error rate itself. Given a predefined error tolerance $p_L^*$, the protocol determines at a chosen confidence level whether the device executes the target circuit at a logical error rate below $p_L^*$. The method relies on trap circuits, copies of the target with every magic state replaced by a stabilizer state, whose outcomes are deterministic and which, being indistinguishable from the target to stochastic Pauli noise, fail at the same rate. We illustrate the protocol in Steane-code simulations of a magic state injection gadget and a quantum Fourier transform.

title: Realistic simulation of universal multiport interferometers with losses within a Gaussian formalism
summary: Photonic technologies are among the leading platform contenders for demonstrating quantum advantage. Nevertheless, photon losses represent the major hurdle for the realization of a fault-tolerant optical quantum computer, and the need for an accurate characterization of this phenomenon is crucial for classical simulations of quantum algorithms on noisy backends. The noisy regime would require the simulation of the algorithm on a Fock backend or rather assuming the a priori hypothesis on the uniformity of the optical losses, which may lead to wrong predictions about the outcome from the algorithm on a cerain hardware. We propose a Gaussian model that can reproduce a lossy dynamics through the experimental characterization of imperfect interferometers, yielding the corresponding mean vector and the covariance matrix. Such model can be adapted to any continuous-variable architecture (spatial or time-bin encoded) and for both the Gaussian boson sampling or general-dyne based algorithms. Eventually, we quantify the drift of optical losses from being uniform throughout the multiport interferometer by a numerical simulation. This work proposes a blueprint for future characterizations, tailor-suited for specific devices and architectures, as well as for potential error correction and mitigation techniques, and it paves the way for realistic simulations of quantum algorithms on NISQ optical platforms.

title: Architecting Instruction Execution for Scalable Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
summary: Scaling fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) requires orchestrating millions of operations continuously across a tightly coupled classical-quantum control stack. A critical challenge in this orchestration is determining the optimal hardware-software boundary, i.e., the Quantum Instruction Set Architecture (QISA). We focus on cryogenic, fixed-connectivity qubit platforms, such as superconducting and topological Majorana qubits. For these, existing QISA choices either operate at too low a level, violating cryogenic thermal budgets at scale, or at too high a level, imposing unrealizable complexity on the control engine. To reason about these tradeoffs, we introduce the ARIES instruction set hierarchy, which categorizes QISAs into distinct abstraction levels. To systematically evaluate these levels, we develop an end-to-end evaluation toolflow featuring a cycle-accurate classical driver and hardware engine simulator. Using eight quantum applications across superconducting and topological qubit platforms, we measure instruction bandwidth, transceiver power dissipation, and measurement processing overheads. We demonstrate that while physical-level abstractions exceed the thermal limits of dilution refrigerators by orders of magnitude, canonical-level abstractions significantly underestimate hardware routing congestion and execution runtimes. title: Cyclotomic Structure and Exact Recurrences in Floquet Many-Body Quantum Dynamics
summary: Periodically driven quantum systems exhibit a wide range of complex dynamics, including chaos. Yet, at special parameter values, their evolution can recur exactly. Several quantum protocols have recently been proposed that exploit exact Floquet recurrences to demonstrate genuine quantum advantage. Such recurrences can be studied through the arithmetic structure of the Floquet unitary. In this work, we establish a necessary and sufficient arithmetic criterion for exact recurrence and determine the minimal recurrence period when one exists. Because recurrence is a global property of the unitary, it holds for every initial state. Applying our framework requires only knowledge of the number field associated with the Hamiltonian parameters. We demonstrate the method using the kicked Ising chain, establishing exact recurrences in both Clifford and non-Clifford regimes. We further show that, in the recurrent non-Clifford regime, magic--a resource for quantum computation--is generated at intermediate times and undergoes exact periodic revivals enforced by the recurrence of the full Floquet unitary. By connecting number theory, quantum many-body dynamics, and quantum information, our work shows that exact recurrence extends beyond Clifford circuits and opens new avenues for magic generation and quantum hardware benchmarking.

title: On the Computational Complexity of Blind Quantum Machine Learning
summary: Can quantum advantages in computational efficiency coexist with quantum advantages in privacy? In this paper, we construct and use MasonQ, a universal brickwork transpiler, to answer this question with a resounding yes. We approach this question by bridging two seemingly disparate paradigms: universal blind quantum computation (UBQC), based on measurement-based quantum computation, and quantum machine learning (QML) algorithms such as the Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd (HHL) algorithm and quantum recommendation systems. We provide new upper bounds on the depth of UBQC brickwork graphs, establishing that $D = \mathcal{O}(ωn)$, where $ω$ is the circuit width and $n$ its computational gate complexity. This is enabled by our newly developed transpiler MasonQ, which maps arbitrary quantum circuits to computational brickwork graph states. Given an optimal Qiskit circuit as input, we prove optimality (up to logarithmic corrections) of the MasonQ transpiler in terms of asymptotic scaling of the total brickwork graph width and depth after decomposition into bricks, enabling systematic cost analyses of blind implementations in near-term experiments and asymptotic regimes. Leveraging MasonQ, we derive depth bounds for several representative blind quantum machine learning (B-QML) algorithms, including the quantum Fourier transform, the HHL algorithm, recommendation systems, and quantum transformers. title: Error-Corrected QRAM Queries with One-Fault-Tolerant \texttt{CSWAP} Gates
summary: Quantum random-access memory (QRAM) enables coherent queries to classical data. However, the \(O(N)\) qubits required for a memory with \(N=2^n\) addresses make QRAM appear vulnerable to noise. Though bucket-brigade routing provides intrinsic noise resilience to reduce the error in QRAM, improving the fidelity of QRAM queries is still an important and challenging problem. We introduce a low-overhead protection framework for bucket-brigade QRAM with two complementary components. First, we propose a one-fault-tolerant repeat-until-success logical controlled-SWAP gate using the \([[4,2,2]]\) code under erasure noise channel. Interleaved erasure checks and local recovery correct every single erasure, so the leading logical failure probability is second order in the physical erasure error rates. Second, we exploit validity constraints of bucket-brigade routing to define local parity checks directly on the router states, without adding extra data qubits to create code redundancy. Under bit-flip noise, minimum-weight perfect matching with noiseless syndrome measurements corrects single interior faults, while open spatial boundaries retain a first-order contribution in the residual bit-flip rate. Monte Carlo simulations confirm quadratic suppression for the protected controlled-SWAP and improved depth scaling for decoded QRAM router-state snapshots. The two codes admit a concatenated realization in which the inner code supplies erasure protection and the outer code optionally correct

title: Time-Domain Observables for Resonant Scattering in Quantum Simulations of Lattice Gauge Theory
summary: Quantum computing may allow unprecedented access to nonequilibrium quantum dynamics, including problems of interest in particle physics, like the real-time development of scattering processes. Although fault-tolerant simulations at scale are still in the future, recent advancements toward early fault-tolerant simulations motivate building increasingly elaborate benchmark problems in order to assess state-of-the-art capabilities and test new algorithms and observables. In this work, we study glueball scattering on a line-of-plaquettes lattice in pure $SU(3)$ lattice gauge theory. We characterize scattering of the lowest-energy glueball states using classical exact diagonalization methods, identifying the continuum resonance structure using real-time simulations and approximate analytic methods, and we propose time-domain observables for extracting properties of the resonance from quantum simulations. We furthermore construct a toy model that shares the spectral features of the lattice gauge theory and demonstrate extraction of the observables. Feasibility on near-term hardware is demonstrated through simulation of a resonant collision of this toy model on Quantinuum System Model $\texttt{H2-2}$, with a 14-plaquette chain encoded in 28 qubits. The Trotterized circuit after optimization and compression requires $\sim 25n$ entangling gates for $n$ Trotter steps.

title: Fast charging of quantum batteries assisted by nonlinear couplings
summary: Charger-mediated quantum batteries offer promising opportunities for efficient energy transfer and storage at the quantum level, with potential advantages beyond their classical counterparts. Here, we theoretically demonstrate that nonlinear charger-battery interactions can substantially accelerate the charging of quantum batteries. In the weak-driving regime, sufficiently strong nonlinear coupling can dominate over the effect of dephasing and significantly reduce the charging time. In the strong- and optimal-driving regimes, where the optimal driving strength maximizes the steady-state ergotropy in the linear-coupling regime, nonlinear coupling gives rise to a new optimum in the charging time beyond that of the linear-coupling regime, accompanied by nearly critically damped dynamics. Remarkably, even in the absence of external driving, nonlinear coupling alone can substantially reduce the charging time, providing an alternative route toward fast battery charging. Our results establish nonlinear charger-battery coupling as an effective resource for accelerating quantum-battery charging and broaden the scope of interaction-enabled quantum advantages in energy transfer and storage.

title: From Syndromes to Computation: A General Framework for Logical Operations in Quantum Error-Correcting Codes
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires error-correcting codes that not only protect quantum information but also support useful logical operations with practical physical realizations. Here we develop a general framework in which the stabilizer syndromes of commuting Pauli rotations directly organize logical-gate design. We derive an exact codespace-preservation condition valid at arbitrary rotation angles, providing a common stabilizer-level description for CSS and non-CSS codes and for both Clifford and non-Clifford operations. A particularly useful equal-syndrome specialization reduces Clifford gate design to stabilizer factorization, yields a general generator weight bound of $\lceil d/2\rceil$ for distance-$d$ codes, and systematically extends to logical rotations higher in the Clifford hierarchy. Applied to bivariate-bicycle (BB) and non-CSS Mirror qLDPC codes, the framework gives explicit low-weight Clifford and controlled-phase gates. Our implementations yield new low-weight gates, including an addressed $T$ gate on the $[[16,4,4]]$ BB code, $T$-type rotations on the $[[64,8,8]]$ BB code, and CCZ-, CS-, and $T$-type operations on the $[[36,6,6]]$ Mirror code. We also develop analytic constructions using Clifford algebra bases, which turn the syndrome constraints into explicit algebraic relations and provide a systematic route to logical addressability. We use this approach to analytically construct addressed CNOT, SWAP, controlled, and CCZ-type gates on recursive

title: Local error correction prolongs time-crystalline memory
summary: Discrete time crystals are non-equilibrium phases of matter with spatiotemporal order and a response that breaks the time-translation symmetry of a periodic external drive. Interactions, spatial disorder and correlated random driving can in theory stabilize this order. In experiments, however, coupling to the environment limits the time crystal lifetime. Here we use stochastic local bit-flip error correction to prolong the time-crystalline response of a driven, spatially disordered two-dimensional Ising model on a superconducting quantum processor, using a repetition code with distances three and five on a honeycomb lattice with up to 68 physical qubits. Even though ancilla qubits, midcircuit syndrome measurements and decoding increase the required quantum and classical resources, the stochastic drive increases the memory decay time by a factor of up to two. At late times we observe that recovery stabilizes spatial order across the lattice. The spin-configuration distributions explain this separation, as recovery suppresses disagreeing bonds while broadening occupies completely reversed states. Syndrome measurements without correction accelerate the memory decay, demonstrating the importance of conditional correction. Our results show that local bit-flip error correction can preserve time-crystalline memory over more drive cycles than the bare dynamics.

title: Distance Prediction for Quantum Codes
summary: The distance of a quantum code is a fundamental metric that dictates its error-correction capability. While quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) families such as Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes offer a promising pathway to low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computing, computing their distance is challenging. Current exact solvers and even search heuristics that provide a distance upper bound suffer from severe computational bottlenecks, restricting the discovery of optimal codes. In this paper, we construct a dataset of BB codes with corresponding distance upper bounds obtained through high-budget heuristic searches. We introduce BB-Net, an attention-based neural network architecture for predicting the distance of BB codes. It achieves 96.39% accuracy on the reference distances in the test set, compared with 94.86% for state-of-the-art heuristics with a budget of up to $10^{4}$ times more computational runtime. On a subset with certified exact distances, BB-Net achieves 98.94%. By relieving the distance-calculation bottleneck, BB-Net enables faster screening of large code spaces, particularly in ML-driven search pipelines, and thereby can accelerate the discovery of novel quantum error-correcting codes, an important capability for advancing scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing. Our code is publicly available: https://github.com/NadavSc/BBNet

title: Methods for Automated Equivalence Checking of Quantum Error-Correction Codes
summary: Quantum error-correction code and circuit construction is an active field of research, motivating automated methods for identifying equivalent designs. We develop and evaluate automated strategies for deciding whether two descriptions of quantum error-correction codes are equivalent under specified transformations. We formalize permutation equivalence for stabilizer and CSS codes and local-Clifford equivalence for stabilizer codes within a unified framework that separates physical from representation freedom. We develop three decision strategies (group-action search, isomorphism-based methods, and constraint solving), together with invariants and signatures for preprocessing. The empirical evaluation shows that no paradigm dominates across equivalence notions, code families, and parameter ranges. We therefore combine their complementary strengths in input-dependent hybrid checkers following a staged Refute-Refine-Decide architecture. Mean hybrid runtimes remain below 10 s for most evaluated structured-code cases with $n \leq 37$; for inequivalent code instances with $n=144$, they are about 310 s for permutation and 16 s for local-Clifford equivalence.

title: PPVM: A Circuit Simulation Framework for Digital Twins of Quantum Processors
summary: Quantum computers are approaching the early fault-tolerant regime. Verifying the next generation of quantum hardware requires joint emulation of the quantum processor, hardware noise, and classical control and decoding logic. We introduce the Programmable Pauli Virtual Machine (PPVM), an open-source framework for digital twins of quantum processors. PPVM unifies Pauli propagation and generalized tableau simulation under a common abstraction within a single virtual machine. Its bytecode supports arbitrary classical control flow, with measurement-conditioned feed-forward available in the generalized tableau backend. For neutral-atom hardware, we derive independent and correlated atom-loss channels and integrate them into both backends. We demonstrate loss-aware magic state distillation on over a thousand physical qubits and integration with classical decoding through Bloqade QEC Studio.

title: Experimental Benchmarking of a 256-Qubit Room-Temperature NV-Diamond Quantum Processor with an Optically Programmable Biomolecular Quantum Bus
summary: We report Zeus-256, a room-temperature nitrogen-vacancy (NV) diamond processor with 256 simultaneously active processor-level logical qubits arranged in a 16 x 16 array. Each logical qubit combines an NV electron-spin ensemble with nuclear-spin memory and ancillary resources. OpenQASM 2.0 circuits are transpiled into RFSoC-controlled microwave, radio-frequency, optical, timing, measurement and bus-configuration sequences. An optically programmable proprietary protein-chromophore layer with an internal metastable-triplet spin mediator provides a reconfigurable biomolecular quantum bus for local and long-range interactions. Benchmarks cover QFT, GHZ entanglement, Grover search, arithmetic, variational, neural-network, graph-state and Shor-family circuits. Factor recovery is reported for 11 integers of 8-84 bits, with 10 attempts per instance; the 84-bit endpoint uses 256 qubits and 40,250,342 reported gates, with a reported execution time of 551.694 ms. Bell-CHSH measurements yield S = 2.8008 +/- 0.0446. Three-qubit Grover search returns the marked state in 958 of 1,024 shots (93.55%), compared with an ideal reference of 94.53%. A separate 30,000-shot population-and-parity protocol yields fixed-phase GHZ+ fidelity of 99.8960%, an estimated standard error of 0.2885 percentage points and a conservative physical 95% interval of [98.2342%, 100%]. Timing metrics are partial and do not establish quantum advantage. Scaling to 9,984 processor-level logical qubits is an engineering targ

title: Lifting: Quantum State Discrimination Framework for Mid-Circuit Measurements
summary: Quantum computing promises new capabilities beyond classical computation. Mid-circuit measurements (MCMs) enable error correction and outcome-dependent control, but their reliability is limited by noise on superconducting hardware. These operations depend on accurate quantum state discrimination (QSD), which assigns measured signals to state labels. Neural network-based (NN-based) QSD improves this assignment, yet its error remains bounded below by the Bayes risk of the available readout distributions. A complementary challenge is state deterioration as successive measurements accumulate and circuit execution advances, making static calibration less representative of the workload. We present Lifting, a QSD framework that addresses both challenges through repetition encoding, neural decoding, and in situ calibration. Encoding supplies joint in-phase and quadrature (I-Q) readout signals from the target and auxiliary qubits, while contextual calibration trains the decoder for the conditions encountered during execution. Our theoretical analysis shows that retaining additional channels from a fixed joint distribution cannot increase Bayes risk and establishes sufficient conditions for contraction of an overlap-based upper bound. Experiments across three IBM processors evaluate the framework on repeated stabilizer measurement, parity-check, and teleportation workloads.

title: Logical gate set tomography
summary: Quantum error correction (QEC) can strongly suppress noise, but predicting whether a computation succeeds requires understanding not only how much effective noise persists after QEC, but what form that noise takes. To thoroughly characterize this noise, we introduce logical gate set tomography (``logical GST''). Logical GST produces detailed representations of noisy logical operations that can be used to derive higher-level metrics, such as gate fidelity and diamond distance, and to test for non-Markovian and coherent logical errors. We use logical GST to obtain the first full, self-consistent characterization of a universal single-qubit logical gate set, implemented in the seven-qubit Steane code using Quantinuum System Model H1, a 20-qubit trapped-ion quantum processor. In the experimental data from H1, logical GST identified predominantly logical Pauli-stochastic errors, found no evidence of logical non-Markovianity, and detected weak potential signatures of coherent logical error. By contrast, higher-shot datasets generated with Quantinuum's detailed system emulator, identify mechanisms for weak but statistically significant logical non-Markovianity and strong evidence of coherent logical error. Finally, we use logical GST to perform error attribution with the system emulator, revealing how specific physical error sources shape logical error mechanisms.

title: A modular quantum computer based on Cornucopia codes
summary: Ultra-high-rate quantum error correction codes store many logical qubits in a single code block with few physical qubits. A fault-tolerant quantum computer, however, also requires a universal set of logical operations on individually addressable logical qubits, and the ancilla overhead of these operations may erode the advantage of the high encoding rate. Here, we propose the Cornucopia architecture, in which a universal set of logical operations is implemented at low overhead for the Cornucopia codes. In particular, we focus on the [[2844,1426,18]] Cornucopia code as an example and introduce a modular quantum computer built from such code blocks connected by bridges. Each block stores 1,426 logical qubits and serves as a universal logical processor. Exploiting the code's translation symmetry, we construct a family of reusable gadgets that individually address 1,422 logical qubits within each block. These gadgets support three universal logical instruction sets: basic, high-throughput and fixed-extractor. Excluding magic-state factories, a module with sufficient workspace to execute any instruction in the basic set requires an average of 4.1 physical qubits per logical qubit, compared with 3.0 for memory alone. The architecture thus preserves the resource advantage of ultra-high-rate quantum memory while enabling universal logical computation, providing a route towards low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computers.

title: Quantum-classical algorithm interpolation for spatial search
summary: Quantum-walk algorithms can quadratically reduce the dependence of spatial search on the classical hitting time $\mathrm{HT}$. Realising this speedup using standard quantum-walk algorithms, however, requires deep coherent circuits, limiting their applicability on near-term and early fault-tolerant quantum devices. We derive a parameterised family of hybrid quantum-classical spatial search algorithms that continuously interpolates between the classical and fully coherent quantum regimes, trading off circuit depth for total query complexity. For any $γ\in[0,1]$, our algorithms use circuits of depth $\widetilde{O}(\mathrm{HT}^{γ/2})$ and find a marked vertex with constant success probability at total cost $\widetilde{O}(\mathrm{HT}^{1-γ}\mathsf{S} + \mathrm{HT}^{1-γ/2}(\mathsf{U} + \mathsf{C}))$, where $\mathsf{S}$, $\mathsf{U}$, and $\mathsf{C}$ denote the setup, update, and checking costs, respectively. We also derive an optimal continuous depth-query trade-off for fixed-point amplitude amplification, providing a potential building block for other hybrid designs.

title: Gap-Priced $|T\rangle$-States: Dynamic $|T\rangle$ Post-Selection and Budget-Aware Factory Provisioning
summary: Magic $|T\rangle$-state preparation dominates the cost of fault-tolerant quantum computation on surface codes, yet cultivation and distillation are typically provisioned statically, leaving much of the program's error budget unused. We present Gap-Priced $|T\rangle$ States (GP$|T\rangle$-S), a lattice surgery scheduler and factory allocator that co-optimizes both methods under a total $T$-error budget. GP$|T\rangle$-S uses the complementary gap of each cultivated state as a fidelity estimate and dynamically adjusts the cultivation gap cutoff, converting budget slack into speed by giving the scheduler control over the cultivation post-selection. GP$|T\rangle$-S also characterizes distillation factories by size, $|T\rangle$-state production rate, and budget slack, and introduces cultivating factories that embed cultivation within routing channels, achieving fidelities otherwise requiring two-level distillation at a single-level footprint. GP$|T\rangle$-S organizes these characterizations into a factory catalog, and performs distillation factory allocation over this catalog in tandem with the gap cutoff using dynamic-programming to achieve one of i) minimum spacetime volume, ii) minimum execution time, or iii) minimum space overhead, all within a user-provided $T$-error budget. title: Dynamical Decoupling of Nonclassical States in a Biased-Noise Spin Qudit
summary: Encoding quantum information in $d$-dimensional systems (qudits) with $d>2$ offers appealing new directions for resource-efficient quantum computing. However, protecting the coherence of nonclassical qudit resource states remains an open challenge. Dynamical decoupling (DD) is a well-established technique for extending coherence, but its application to qudits is hindered by the quadratic scaling of the decoupling sequence overhead with the dimension $d$. As a result, demonstrations of qudit DD have so far been limited to low-dimensional qudits. Here, we show that noise-biased qudits enable a nontrivial reduction of this overhead, for example, from quadratic to linear. We perform qudit DD on a model $d=8$ qudit, the nuclear spin of an antimony donor in silicon. We benchmark DD performance on highly nonclassical states such as uniform superpositions, cat states, and Haar random states and measure coherence improvements up to a factor $5$ to $10$. For a spin-cat error correction code, continuous DD extends the coherence time of the logical superposition $|+\rangle_L$ to $225$~ms, compared to $19$~ms under free evolution and $85$~ms with a Hahn echo. This improvement shows that DD sequences tailored to a system's noise bias can significantly enhance the lifetime of encoded logical qubits.

title: Quantum-enhanced phase interrogation of a fiber-optic strain sensor
summary: Fiber-optic sensors enable high-sensitivity measurements of various physical parameters. Here, we demonstrate a quantum-enhanced interrogation of an all-fiber-optic Fabry-Perot resonator, employing entangled two-photon interference to probe directly strain-induced optical phase shifts. The resonator is interrogated by a narrow-linewidth laser that is frequency-locked to its resonance mode, thereby exploiting the cavity's inherent sensitivity to variations in the fiber length. To access the phase fluctuations transferred to the interrogation field due to external perturbations on the sensor, we implement an in-fiber Mach-Zehnder interferometer readout. This configuration allows the sensor to operate both with classical coherent light and with entangled photon pairs generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion. Harnessing two-photon entangled states corresponding to an N = 2 NOON state, we experimentally demonstrate a reduction of the measurement noise below the standard quantum limit. These results provide clear evidence of the quantum advantage in enhancing fiber-optic sensors under practical constraints on optical power.

title: Scalable Tomography of Coherent Noise via Stabilizer-Code Polarization
summary: Coherent errors accumulate linearly rather than diffusively, making them invisible to Pauli-twirl-based char- acterization. It poses a central challenge for quantum error correction, yet its characterization typically requires multi-qubit process tomography whose cost grows exponentially with system size. We show that measurement- free error correction projects arbitrary few-qubit coherent noise onto a fixed single-logical-qubit effective chan- nel, enabling tomography at constant cost. Exploiting the polarization effects of bit-flip and phase-flip codes, we construct a concatenated effective-channel fingerprint and prove, by a parity-based contradiction argument, that the observation map is globally injective over a prescribed coherent-noise family; hence the underlying noise parameters are uniquely recovered without any sparsity or low-rank assumptions. The recovered coherent noise model can be fed into decoding algorithms; relative to independent noise priors, we expect this to reduce the logical error rate for surface-code decoders. The protocol offers a scalable route to coherent-noise identification whenever the noise admits a moderate-dimensional parameterization.

title: Quantum Folding in Chebyshev-Based Quantum Subspace Diagonalization
summary: Quantum subspace diagonalization (QSD) with a Krylov space spanned by Chebyshev polynomials of the Hamiltonian is a natural ground-state method for fault-tolerant quantum computers, but every guarantee it offers---convergence rate, noise floor, and the cost of turning its classical output back into a physical state---is controlled by the overlap of the reference state with the true ground state, which decays exponentially with system size for any product state and non-trivial Hamiltonian. We propose quantum folding: for a system governed by a local Hamiltonian, seed the QSD with the product of the ground states of its subsystems, which differs from the target only through the interface terms. We prove a nonasymptotic error bound for the Chebyshev QSD that is linear in the measurement noise, by transplanting Kirby's effective-Hamiltonian analysis to the Chebyshev--Krylov basis, and identify the block-encoding rescaling of the Hamiltonian as a parameter of the guarantee. Exact simulations of antiferromagnetic Heisenberg chains show that the folded reference state reduces the Krylov dimension for a given accuracy severalfold and lowers the error under noise by two to five orders of magnitude relative to the Néel state. We show how the Ritz vector is prepared as a physical state and that the ground-state generation probability obeys a tight ceiling set by the overlap, so that recursive folding prepares ground states at polynomial cost. Taken together, these results allow for a sc

title: Deterministic and Programmable Fusion for Scalable Generation of Photonic Graph States
summary: Entanglement in multiphoton graph states is an important resource with various applications, such as measurement-based quantum computing and memory-less quantum repeaters. While some primitive instances have been successfully prepared, scalable generation of large-scale graph states with programmable connections remains an outstanding challenge. Fusion provides a promising "divide-and-conquer" approach by linking smaller resource states into larger, more complex graphs. However, its practical scalability has been limited by the probabilistic nature of conventional fusion protocols, which necessitates extensive hardware overhead and feed-forward resources to achieve deterministic outcomes. Here, we introduce and experimentally demonstrate a deterministic fusion operation with built-in error mitigation, capable of connecting small time-bin-encoded cluster states--originally generated on-demand from a quantum emitter--into larger, reconfigurable photonic graph states of increased sizes. The fusion operation is realized by nondestructively projecting pairs of flying microwave photonic qubits into Bell states using superconducting circuits with in-situ programmability. Crucially, the protocol features active reset and reuse of matter qubits during graph state generation, thereby circumventing the coherence constraints of the quantum emitter and enabling the generation of genuine multipartite entanglement across 13 photonic qubits. Our results establish a scalable framework for pho

title: A low-cost compact muon detector for millikelvin operation
summary: Ionizing radiation produces correlated errors in superconducting qubits, posing some challenges to quantum error correction. In addition, it causes background events in other superconducting cryogenic devices, such as kinetic inductance detectors and superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors. Cosmic muons are a component of this background that can only be partly shielded against at ground level, but can be tagged by an independent detector inside the cryostat, so that the affected data can be vetoed, or the muon tags incorporated into error correction. We present a low-cost, compact muon detector consisting of two plastic scintillator modules, each read out by a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM), operated in coincidence. We characterize the SiPMs from room temperature down to 10 mK, including the breakdown and upper-limit voltages that define the operating bias range. Operated as a muon counter, the detector measures a coincidence rate that, as expected, is independent of temperature within uncertainties and agrees with analytical and Monte Carlo predictions. Below approximately 8 K, each muon event produces two pulses, one narrow and one broad, an effect that, to our knowledge, has not been reported before. Coincidences with an independent muon detector outside the cryostat confirm that muons are still counted reliably in this regime. By studying the appearance of double pulses as a function of temperature and magnetic field up to 4.5 T, we find a behavior consistent wi

title: Petz Recovery through a Single Polar Transformation for Approximate Quantum Error Correction
summary: The Petz recovery map provides a near optimal decoder for approximate quantum error correction, but its inverse square-root normalization complicates circuit implementation. We use the polar structure of the Petz recovery isometry to implement recovery through a single quantum singular value transformation (QSVT). We give explicit block-encoding circuits and an extended recovery isometry that yields approximate Petz recovery without postselection. We bound the diamond distance between the approximate and ideal Petz encoding-recovery channels in terms of a spectrum-weighted loss, which provides a channel specific objective for optimizing the QSVT angles. Uniform polynomial approximation yields an asymptotic error bound that decays exponentially with the number of QSVT iterations, at a rate controlled by the smallest nonzero scaled singular value. Applications to Haar-random encoding and the Hayden-Preskill protocol illustrate the tradeoff between circuit depth and recovery accuracy and place existing scrambling decoders within a common Petz recovery framework.

title: Logical CCZ state cultivation
summary: Logical CCZ states enable Toffoli gates, a central building block of fault-tolerant quantum arithmetic. We introduce an end-to-end protocol for direct CCZ-state preparation on bivariate tricycle and bicycle (BT/BB) codes. Our factory combines the cup-product CCZ gates native to BT codes with two novel ingredients, both enabled by engineering the logical coupling between BT and BB codes through projection-preserving lifts. Index-2 lifted BB ancillas enable selective $Z$-basis initialization, allowing the native cup-product gates to directly prepare two disjoint logical CCZ states. The prepared CCZ states are faithfully transferred to index-3 lifted BB memories with high code distance. We use decoder-based postselection to obtain high-fidelity output states with low overhead. We perform exact simulations of our factory under a circuit-level noise model motivated by neutral-atom hardware, obtaining joint infidelities of $1.84\times10^{-5}$ at $21.94\%$ acceptance and $4.10\times10^{-7}$ at $8.89\%$ acceptance for single-qubit, CZ, and CCZ error rates of $0.01\%$, $0.1\%$, and $0.5\%$, respectively. At the output-infidelity target of our smallest factory, its estimated spacetime cost per CCZ state is lower than that of $T$-state cultivation followed by CCZ conversion, providing an efficient route to logical CCZ states for fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: Quantum prepare-and-measure scenarios: concepts and methods
summary: Prepare-and-measure scenarios are among the simplest and most widely used settings for quantum communication. A sender prepares a physical system in one of several possible states, which a receiver then measures. Despite this simple structure, these scenarios offer a rich framework for exploring the differences between classical and quantum communication, revealing quantum advantages, and developing protocols for quantum cryptography and device certification. In this tutorial, we give a ground-up introduction to prepare-and-measure scenarios and the methods used to study them. We introduce different frameworks for constraining and characterising communication, with an emphasis on semi-device-independent approaches to quantum information. We also cover modern convex-optimisation techniques for characterising the correlations achievable in these scenarios and illustrate how these tools can be applied in practice. Our aim is to give newcomers the conceptual and technical foundations needed to approach the current literature and apply prepare-and-measure methods in their own research. We conclude with a discussion of open problems and directions for future work.

title: Perfect and peak state transfer on IBM quantum hardware
summary: We run continuous-time quantum walks with perfect and peak state transfer on a present-day superconducting quantum processor, IBM Quantum's $156$-qubit Heron device ibm_kingston, deliberately without error correction or error mitigation. Perfect state transfer and its relaxations have been studied extensively in algebraic graph theory, where one can prove exactly which graphs move a quantum state from one vertex to another with probability one (or with the largest probability the graph allows, in the case of peak state transfer), and at what time. Our experiments cover perfect state transfer on the hypercubes $Q_2 = C_4$ and $Q_3$, and on the Hamming-weighted paths $\mathrm{HP}_n$, the equitable-partition quotients of the hypercubes $Q_n$, for $n$ up to $20$; peak state transfer on the $X_n$ family for $n$ up to $11$; and, for comparison, moving the state along a path of qubits by a sequence of SWAP gates.

title: Practical wavelength selection for quantum-augmented networks over shared optical fiber
summary: In a quantum augmented network, sharing optical fiber with classical traffic requires quantum wavelength selection to balance logical fidelity, block acceptance, and classical data reception. Here we develop a wavelength-selection framework for an error-corrected three-stage quantum communication protocol. Under a thermal-background model with independent errors, an ideal one-photon receiver, and ideal recovery, we derive an accepted qubit channel and a key-independent lower bound on logical entanglement fidelity. Combining this bound with block acceptance gives an entanglement-fidelity yield bound, which we maximize over evaluated wavelengths subject to fidelity and classical link-budget requirements. For the Steane [[7,1,3]] code at 5 km per traversal and -10 dBm per classical channel, the largest fidelity certificate occurs near 1537 nm, whereas the largest yield bound occurs near 1551 nm. Along the 1.25 Gb/s classical link budget with 0.2% base error, the optimized yield bound falls below 10^-6 near 10 km per traversal, while fidelity remains certified at 0.99 or higher at longer spans. These results distinguish fidelity and yield constraints and identify certified operating regions for quantum-augmented networks sharing optical fiber.

title: Stitched surface codes: planar concatenation through GHZ corridors
summary: We present a fault-tolerant quantum-memory architecture that concatenates four distance-t rotated surface-code patches with the [[4,2,2]] outer code, encoding two logical qubits at code distance d = 2t in a physical footprint of N < 2(2t+1)^2 qubits on a square lattice with nearest-neighbor connectivity. The outer-code stabilizer generators XXXX and ZZZZ, each of physical weight 4t, are measured in situ via verified Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) ancillae distributed through narrow corridors between adjacent patches, without lattice surgery or long-range gates. The outer-code gadgets introduce hyperedge fault mechanisms, but by design each decomposes into graphlike components, so the complete syndrome is decoded by a single minimum-weight-perfect-matching pass. Circuit-level simulations show logical error rates that scale as p^t, consistent with distance-2t protection. Finally, we implement the construction experimentally on a 105-qubit Willow superconducting processor in both the ZZ and XX memory bases. With the correlated-matching decoder, increasing the code distance from d = 4 to d = 6 reduces the block logical error rate by a factor of 1.52. The construction thus provides a near-term testbed for concatenated architectures beyond the standard surface code.

title: Remote Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill Entanglement Generation between Trapped Ions
summary: Distributing entanglement directly between error-corrected logical qubits is an important capability for scalable quantum networks. We propose a heralded protocol for generating remote entanglement between Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill qubits encoded in the motional modes of spatially separated trapped ions, using the internal electronic states to interface the motional qubits with emitted photons. We derive the protocol for single-rail and polarization photonic encodings and evaluate the effects of finite GKP squeezing, photon loss, photon recoil, motional heating, and motional dephasing on the decoded logical state. Moreover, we numerically analysed the fidelity of distributed logical Bell-pair fidelity. We find that one can achieve more than 95% of fidelity in the realistic situation. The protocol combines motional-control and photonic-networking operations that have already been demonstrated in trapped-ion experiments.

title: Quantum-compatible Riemannian conjugate gradient for ground-state preparation
summary: Riemannian optimization provides a natural geometric framework for designing quantum algorithms for ground-state preparation, most notably through quantum imaginary-time evolution. However, existing geometry-aware approaches primarily employ steepest-descent updates, leaving more advanced methods from classical Riemannian optimization largely unexplored. In this work, we introduce quantum conjugate gradient descent (QCGD), a quantum-compatible implementation of Riemannian conjugate gradient that combines the steepest descent direction with information retained from previous search directions. In our numerical experiments, the proposed approach achieves faster convergence per iteration than the baseline double-bracket quantum imaginary-time evolution (DB-QITE) algorithm, and we quantify the associated circuit cost with gate counts produced by Qrisp. This improvement, however, comes at the cost of increased circuit depth for each update step, revealing a trade-off between convergence rate and implementation complexity. Nevertheless, since the circuit depth for those algorithms grows exponentially with the number of iterations, the proposed method may offer practical advantages, particularly in the early fault-tolerant regime.

title: Superconducting circuits host two-level systems with lifetimes exceeding one second
summary: Understanding the microscopic environment of superconducting qubits is a central challenge for quantum technologies. Parasitic two-level systems (TLSs) of various microscopic origins are ubiquitous and limit qubit performance through decoherence, frequency drifts, and leakage. Recently, long-lived TLSs with lifetimes exceeding those of state-of-the-art qubits have been shown to induce correlated qubit dynamics, with direct implications for quantum error correction. Here, we perform wide-band quantum-jump correlation spectroscopy on flux-tunable transmon qubits and identify microscopic degrees of freedom that outlive the qubit by orders of magnitude. Pump-probe measurements at varying detunings from these objects reveal intrinsic lifetimes exceeding one second. Their weak coupling to the qubit, in the kilohertz range, is consistent with positional defects described by the standard tunneling model, without excluding other microscopic origins such as magnetic spin impurities or trapped quasiparticles. More broadly, these results establish superconducting qubits as a sensitive probe of exceptionally long-lived microscopic degrees of freedom and open a route toward their controlled access and functionalization.

title: One generation of the Standard Model as a quantum error-correcting code
summary: Together with a right-handed neutrino, the fermions of one generation of the Standard Model are labelled by five bits, a combinatorial structure tied to anomaly cancellation. We make this precise. Anomaly cancellation is the vanishing of a cubic form, the defining property of triorthogonal codes, the quantum error-correcting codes behind magic state distillation. Removing the right-handed neutrino gives a $[[15,1,3]]_p$ code for every prime $p$, including the Bravyi-Kitaev code for $p = 2$. For qutrits it is the unique shortest distance-three triorthogonal code.

title: Bubble-Sort Exchange Networks: Symmetry Selection Rules and Language-Model Distillation on Exchange-Only Spin Chains
summary: On a chain of exchange-coupled quantum dots a Heisenberg exchange pulse of area pi is a SWAP, so the parallel bubble-sort SWAP network of superconducting chains is native to exchange-only (EO) spin qubits, and any other pulse area fuses routing with an entangling interaction. We build a variational "bubble-sort exchange network" (odd-even transposition, one parameter per pulse) and study it as a Born machine read out by Pauli spin blockade. Exchange conserves total spin, so the reachable readout distributions are fixed by the total-spin content of the initial product state. For the two-spin singlet-triplet encoding we derive a selection rule -- outcomes with k triplet pairs are bounded by the initial weight in sectors S <= k (S = 0 excluded for k = 1) -- and prove by a transportation argument that it is also sufficient: the reachable distributions form the polytope cut out by the rule, and its total-variation floor is attained. Products of singlets and T0's forbid whole outcome classes; the Neel state forbids none; the three-spin EO code has no floor. title: Patchwork: automated lattice surgery and space-time partitioning for real-time decoding
summary: We introduce patchwork, a lattice-surgery compiler for arbitrary multi-qubit Pauli measurements on a prescribed narrow-corridor two-dimensional surface-code layout. Systematic geometric rules simplify stabilizer placement and gate scheduling, including for logical $Y$ measurements implemented using twist defects. We introduce measurement circuits and schedules that, together with protruding lobes of $Y$-extension patches, preserve the full effective code distance for all numerically tested code distances. To support parallel decoding, we develop a wavefront algorithm that partitions merged lattice-surgery patches into space-time commit, buffer, and cleanup regions. Simulations of three sequential multi-qubit Pauli measurements acting on ten logical qubits show that staged decoding achieves total failure probabilities close to those of monolithic decoding over the parameters tested. These methods provide an automated framework for fault-tolerant lattice surgery and a route toward scalable, real-time decoding.

title: Energetics of Fault-Tolerant Spin-Qubit Quantum Computation
summary: Semiconductor spin qubits offer a promising route to compact and scalable quantum computers, combining long coherence times in isotopically purified silicon with compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing. Beyond computational speedup, their energy efficiency is an important consideration for future large-scale systems. We evaluate the power and energy requirements of a Loss-DiVincenzo spin-qubit quantum computer by analyzing the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) and benchmarking it against the classical Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). We develop a detailed energy budget, identifying cryogenic cooling as the dominant baseline contribution before quantum error correction (QEC). The comparison between the QFT and the classical FFT reveals that, for any quantum workload operating under a polynomially bounded sampling regime, the crossover in energy consumption occurs at smaller problem sizes than the crossover in execution time. Thus, quantum computing can become energetically competitive before achieving a speedup in execution time. We then incorporate surface-code QEC and analyze the energy costs of QEC cycles, gate synthesis, and decoding. At scale, instrumentation and decoding become dominant contributions, while cryogenic cooling imposes a constraint on scalability. We show that optimizing the control-signal demultiplexing ratio can reduce the overall energy cost by approximately two orders of magnitude. title: Classification of bipartite observables III: simplicity, mixtures and quantum error correction
summary: This is the third of a series of three papers that bring model theory to quantum information. The dividing lines of Shelah's classification theory, which separate the tame first-order theories from the wild ones, become properties of bipartite observables: properties of the expectation values obtained when two independently prepared quantum systems are idealized one after the other. In this paper we focus on simple unstable theories. The Pauli group of quantum error correction, with anticommutation as its relation, has a simple unstable theory, like the random graph. Forking and the Kim--Pillay independence theorem acquire a meaning in stabilizer codes: forking recognizes logical errors, and the independence theorem glues syndromes.

title: Programmable all-to-all entangling gates for cavity-coupled atoms
summary: Fault tolerant quantum computers greatly benefit from having both high fidelity entangling gates and a non-local qubit connectivity. However, most entangling gates for neutral atoms are local, requiring separated atoms to be moved using optical tweezers to yield entanglement between them. Here, we design a high fidelity Mølmer Sørensen-like entangling gate between neutral atoms coupled to a photonic cavity, enabling a programmable all-to-all connectivity through the shared cavity coupling. The gate is both robust to changes in cavity photon number, and enables selective entanglement between any subset of separated atoms through local laser addressing. This eliminates the need to physically move atoms to perform the gate, and therefore motional errors and erasure are suppressed. Using experimentally realistic parameters we demonstrate gate fidelities exceeding $F > 0.99$, with higher fidelities achievable through optimal control of the pump amplitudes.

title: SynDebug: A Framework to Debug Logic Bugs in Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Programs
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) introduces substantial systems-level complexity through quantum error correction (QEC), making debugging FTQC programs challenging. Existing quantum debugging approaches primarily target logical-level circuits and do not naturally support debugging within realistic FTQC execution flows. We present SynDebug, the first systems-level debugging framework for FTQC programs. SynDebug introduces lightweight assertion-based debugging primitives that operate directly within encoded FTQC infrastructures while avoiding additional logical surface area and minimizing temporal overhead. We evaluate SynDebug across multiple QEC code families, code distances, and encoded workloads, including state preparation, entanglement validation, and Shor-style programs. Our results demonstrate that SynDebug enables practical FTQC debugging with an average 1.8% additional circuit depth overhead (0% in most cases) and no measurable increase in the logical error rate, showing that systems-level debugging for large-scale FTQC applications is both feasible and practical.

title: Stability of Quantum LDPC States under Local Pauli Noise
summary: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes have a canonical mixed state---the normalized projector onto the code space---that lies at the intersection of quantum error correction and quantum many-body physics, yet the stability of its information-theoretic structure under local noise remains poorly understood. Recent progress on mixed-state phases of matter has identified the spatial decay of conditional mutual information (CMI) $I(A:C|B)$ as a key diagnostic of such stability, analogous to the role of the spectral gap for quantum ground states. We prove that, for the normalized code-projector state of a $\mathbb{Z}_d$ qLDPC stabilizer code under local Pauli noise, the CMI across a buffer $B$ separating $A$ from $C$ decays exponentially with the width of $B$ in two complementary noise regimes independent of system size. At weak noise, this holds for full-system tripartitions, where correlations between the two sides require an error cluster to cross the buffer, an exponentially unlikely event. At strong noise, exponential decay holds whenever the buffer supports no logical operator, since correlations can persist only along rare chains of buffer qudits that remain informative. Under an additional space-uniformity assumption, we establish the robustness of Levin--Wen topological entropy. title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models
summary: Significant efforts are currently being directed toward the implementation of large-scale quantum information processors, but realizing useful quantum advantage also requires the development of efficient quantum algorithms. While for many practical problems the dominant resource costs are associated with a small set of computational primitives, optimizing them in the quantum setting presents unique challenges, including a reversibility constraint absent from ordinary classical computation. Here we introduce an evolutionary framework in which large language models (LLMs) propose circuit designs and an independent evaluator verifies and scores them. We apply this framework to tasks spanning numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, and number theory. In seven of the eight tasks, the discovered circuits significantly reduce both Toffoli and qubit counts relative to the state of the art. In the eighth, the search discovers a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion. By handling reversibility differently, the architecture makes divsteps -- a classical algorithm previously impractical for reversible integer arithmetic -- viable and substantially improves the Toffoli-qubit trade-off for modular inversion. These results open the door for evaluator-guided LLM co-design of new algorithmic structures for quantum computation.

title: Area Theorems for Quantum Error Correction
summary: The extrinsic information transfer (EXIT) and generalized EXIT (GEXIT) area theorems provide fundamental conservation laws that connect the rate of classical codes to the performance of maximum-a-posteriori decoding on binary memoryless channels. In this work, we generalize these area theorems to quantum error correction. We first develop a coset-entropy formalism for nested linear codes, where the message specifies a coset and encoder randomization selects a codeword within that coset. The area under the resulting coset (G)EXIT function equals the normalized dimension of the quotient. For stabilizer codes, the measured syndrome restricts the Pauli error but does not always determine its logical effect, and the remaining uncertainty is an entropy over logical correction classes. We show that this entropy equals a classical coset entropy associated with the stabilizer group and the Pauli operators that commute with it. The resulting quantum GEXIT function has area equal to the number of encoded qubits per channel use for any stabilizer code, and this applies to the depolarizing channel through its joint four-valued Pauli-error distribution. For CSS codes on the quantum erasure channel and under independent bit- and phase-flip noise, the logical correction problem separates into two binary coset-decoding problems. title: Encodings and Node Architecture: Lessons from the Fault-Tolerant Distributed Transversal Fanout
summary: An encoding choice specifies the quantum error-correcting code used to encode logical qubits at a given node. Different encoding choices may differ in the number of physical qubits, the number of encoded logical qubits, the code distance, and the available fault-tolerant operations. We study different encodings for a distributed transversal fanout operation and look at its implications on node architecture. Our experiments suggest that an encoding with higher distance, even if requiring more ebits, can yield a lower logical error rate for distributed operations, and that ``upgrading'' an encoding prior to distributed operations and having a cache, as part of node architecture, for qubits can be useful for distributed operations.

title: Concrete Functions in Private Simultaneous Quantum Messages: Quantum Advantages and Structural Limitations
summary: Private simultaneous quantum messages (PSQM) provide a minimal model of noninteractive secure multiparty quantum computation, yet their communication complexity for concrete functions remains poorly understood. We show that familiar total functions already exhibit both genuine quantum advantages and strong structural limitations. For three-party equality on $n$-bit inputs, which determines whether the players' $n$-bit strings are identical, we construct an entanglement-assisted protocol with asymptotic communication $(1.633\ldots)n$ qubits, whereas every perfectly correct protocol without prior entanglement requires at least $3n$ qubits. For three-bit majority, one shared GHZ state and one transmitted qubit per player suffice for perfect correctness and perfect privacy, reducing the communication from the optimal classical cost of six bits to three qubits. Three-bit AND behaves differently. No perfectly correct and perfectly private protocol exists when the players share an arbitrary three-qubit state, apply arbitrary local unitary encodings, and transmit one qubit each. However, increasing the local dimension overcomes this obstruction: one shared three-qutrit GHZ state and one transmitted qutrit per player yield a one-shot protocol with total communication $3\log_2 3$. Together with the six-bit classical lower bound, this gives a strict quantum communication advantage. title: Demonstration of Logical Error Suppression in a Surface Code Memory on a Cloud-Accessible IBM Superconducting Processor
summary: Quantum error correction can suppress logical errors exponentially with code distance when physical noise is below threshold. Realizing this on hardware requires tight coordination among quantum gates, mid-circuit measurements, and qubit coherence. Device variation, noise asymmetry, and correlations across space and time complicate the translation of these capabilities into logical error suppression. Here, we study rotated surface-code memory on an IBM Nighthawk r2 processor. Performance varies across tested processor placements, which we attribute to differences in qubit quality. We optimize the code by combining short readout, fused measurement and reset, and an XX echo on data qubits during ancilla readout. Compared with standard readout without reset or echo, the optimized syndrome extraction circuit reduces the median per-round logical error rate by factors of 3.8 in the X basis and 1.4 in the Z basis. In memory experiments of up to 150 rounds, the distance advantage weakens, alongside long-lived correlations that may reflect a persistent error component. Under our optimization recipe, increasing the protected distance from 3 to 6 while holding the other distance fixed reduces the per-round logical error rate from 0.53% to 0.24% in Z memory and from 0.52% to 0.22% in X memory. title: Quantum error correction well below the color code threshold
summary: Quantum error correction enables scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation by suppressing logical errors exponentially with code distance once physical error rates fall below a critical threshold. Here we demonstrate below-threshold operation of triangular color codes with distances $d=3,5,$ and $7$ on Quantinuum's Helios trapped-ion quantum processor. Leveraging both circuit- and hardware- level leakage reduction schemes, we achieve logical error rates as low as $5_{-2}^{+4}\times 10^{-6}$, and demonstrate error suppression by over an order of magnitude, $Λ=12_{-2}^{+3}$, with each successive increase in code distance. Moreover, we demonstrate below threshold scaling of error rates for Clifford two-qubit randomized benchmarking circuits when encoded in $d=3,5$ color codes, achieving logical error rate of $7^{+3}_{-3}\times 10^{-5}$ per logical two-qubit Clifford at distance $5$ with a suppression factor of $Λ=9_{-3}^{+8}$. We compare logical performance for existing near-optimal algorithmic decoders, and both convolutional neural network and transformer-based neural network decoders capable of real-time decoding an order of magnitude faster than the syndrome extraction rate. These results approach the logical error rates required for megaquop-scale quantum computation and indicate that scaled trapped-ion processors could reach application-relevant performance with substantially smaller code blocks than indicated by previous results in other qubit modalities.

title: Nonlocality as a Benchmarking Tool for Quantum Processors
summary: Benchmarking quantum processors is a central task in every roadmap aimed at quantum advantage. Here, we discuss a benchmarking protocol based on the violation of the Svetlichny inequality, which is designed to simulate genuine multipartite nonlocality. We compare it with Mermin's inequality, and present the results of applying this framework to two different quantum processing units -the superconducting system Garnet (from IQM) and the ion-trap system Marmot (from AQT), testing different families of quantum circuits for three to five qubits under identical experimental conditions. We also run simultaneous triplet tests across the full register, including a comparison between GHZ and linear cluster states, to probe how Svetlichny-inequality violations depend on qubit location and calibration. Our results demonstrate that tests based on genuine multipartite nonlocality provide a powerful tool to characterize the collective performance of quantum devices and to guide their calibration and optimization.

title: Optimal robust single-qubit gates in superconducting quantum processors
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires high-fidelity quantum gates that are resilient to control errors and device imperfections. Here, we develop energy-optimal control pulses for single-qubit gates that are simultaneously robust against frequency detuning and waveform inhomogeneities while also suppressing leakage outside the computational subspace. Combining the optimized pulse envelopes with an adaptive control scheme, we experimentally demonstrate optimal robust gates on a superconducting quantum processor. For a gate duration of 90ns, we achieve fidelities above 99.9% for the X gate and 99.6% for Hadamard-type gates. For the X gate, we maintain fidelities above 99.5% for simultaneous drive-amplitude variations up to 20% and qubit detuning up to 4 MHz. This robustness outperforms that of conventional Gaussian pulses by an order of magnitude, without much difference in peak gate fidelity. These results establish a route towards robust single-qubit control in large-scale quantum processors, advancing the development of fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: FTWeave: Composing Logical Execution, Real-Time Decoding, and Magic-State Supply in Tightly Integrated Quantum-Classical Systems
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum applications depend on both decoded measurement information and a continuing supply of magic states. While an operation waits for either, its logical data require protection that produces more syndrome data and decoding work. Architects must provision the quantum and classical parts of the machine together, before complete systems are available to measure. FTWeave is a system-level simulator for this architectural exploration. It accepts OpenQASM 2/3 circuits, CUDA-Q Logical compiler artifacts, Stim circuits, and provider-derived physical inputs through adapters that preserve operation and measurement dependencies. Users bind these inputs to quantum resources, classical processors, memory, communication, and factory configurations. One event timeline determines application progress, resource ownership, and continuing protection. This supplies the system model needed to connect circuit and decoder evidence to application performance. Controlled demand studies and complete multiplier and Ising circuits show why the coupling changes provisioning decisions. A fixed-work approximation predicts a 3.55x multiplier speedup from additional factories where the coupled model gives almost none. Explicit ownership also changes useful capacity: increasing decoder workers alone has no benefit in a storage-constrained case, while increasing workers and feedback entries together gives 4.93x speedup. Selected color and hypergraph-product code mappings take 53-90% longer

title: LiftDiff: Guided Discrete Diffusion for Quantum Code Construction
summary: The realization of fault-tolerant quantum computation relies on Quantum Error-Correcting Codes (QECC). Of particular interest are codes that combine a high encoding rate with sufficient distance. Existing algebraic constructions, such as lifted product (LP) codes, build a large quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) code from a classical base matrix. In this work we introduce LiftDiff, a generative approach to the discovery of QECC. A discrete denoising diffusion model is trained to generate base matrices over the group algebra $\mathbb{F}_2[\mathbb{Z}_\ell]$, which are then expanded into LP codes. The reverse diffusion process is guided by an energy function that evaluates quantum code properties, including girth, degree, sparsity and decoding performance, steering the sampler toward matrices that yield LP codes with favorable parameters. Our method discovers codes with parameters such as $[[169,13,11]]$, $[[143,15,9]]$, and $[[260,24,10]]$, including a $[[247,19,14]]$ code that achieves the highest ${kd^2}/{n}$ among the baselines. Moreover, several discovered codes outperform the Gross code across a broad range of the tested physical error rates under both code-capacity and circuit-level noise.

title: \textit{In situ} certification of multiparticle indistinguishability in a generic interferometer
summary: We propose a scalable and efficient \textit{in situ} method for assessing the multiparticle indistinguishability of identical bosons or fermions in quantum interference experiments on linear interferometers by harnessing quantum parallelism and the bunching/anti-bunching tendencies of these particles. The proposed certification method can be applied to any generic linear interferometer. For particles occupying distinct input ports of a Haar-random unitary interferometer, the number of experimental runs required to attain a prescribed statistical precision is polynomial in the number of particles, the interferometer size, and the inverse precision, with high probability. Our method is robust under losses: for uniform particle losses, the polynomial scaling is preserved when the inverse single-particle survival probability is polynomially bounded. Our scheme is especially suitable for certifying the indistinguishability of single photons in large-scale interference experiments, such as Boson Sampling in the regime of quantum advantage over classical computation.

title: Topological Quantum Gates on FCIs with Bounded Quantum Geometry
summary: Two-band 2D fractional Chern insulators (FCIs) have recently been shown, in principle, to admit unusual anyonic order, associated with Bloch Hopfions localized in momentum space. Here we show that bounding the integrated quantum metric along one primitive Brillouin-zone cycle may refine this topological order to $|C|$ distinct braiding observables, cyclically permuted by lattice translations, for Chern numbers $|C| > 1$. The cyclic structure entails mildly non-abelian braiding phases and otherwise matches the spectral flow exhibited by the FCI's hybrid Wannier states, with the metric bound equivalently a bound on the states' real-space spread. We give a classification of quantum gates in principle implementable on this topological order; among them we find the non-Clifford T-gate and the non-Clifford entangling CCZ-gate. This points to novel pathways to fault-tolerant quantum processes within the known orbital structure of FCIs, potentially informing experimental searches towards hardware for future topological quantum computers.
